items.title: Millions Agree
items.question: An advert claims: 'Millions of people use this shampoo, so it must be good.' This appeals to popularity rather than evidence.
items.correctExplanation: Right — that is argumentum ad populum: a head-count is offered where evidence belongs.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The argument swaps user numbers for actual proof of quality — the textbook appeal to popularity. Millions of people can be wrong, misled, or simply copying each other.
items.lessonContent:
Argumentum ad populum swaps a head-count for evidence: many believe it, therefore it is true.
Popularity tracks spread, not truth — rumours and fashions are popular by design.
The tell is structural: look for numbers of believers standing where reasons should be.
History's scoreboard is humbling — majorities once backed geocentrism and bloodletting.
Share this: next time an advert counts its fans, ask what evidence besides the count is on offer.

items.title: The Dropout Defence
items.question: Dismissing a colleague's budget argument because she failed maths in school commits an ad hominem.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — her school maths marks have no bearing on whether this budget argument holds.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The response targets the person making the argument instead of the argument itself, which is the defining move of an ad hominem. A bad grade decades ago cannot make a valid budget case invalid.
items.lessonContent:
Ad hominem answers an argument by attacking its author — credentials, history, habits.
Its flaw is relevance: the arguer's traits cannot flip a premise from false to true.
The two-part test: is the point about the person, and is it doing the argument's work?
Debate judges watch for exactly this substitution.
Share this: when a debate turns personal, note whose claim is suddenly not being discussed.

items.title: The Scarecrow Tactic
items.question: Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is called a straw man.
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — you build a weaker scarecrow version of their view, then knock it down and claim victory.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The straw man fallacy is precisely this: replace the real position with a distorted, weaker one, then attack that instead. The name comes from fighting a dummy rather than the actual opponent.
items.lessonContent:
A straw man works in two steps: quietly replace the real position with a weaker caricature, then defeat the caricature loudly.
Victory over the copy is presented as victory over the original.
The defence is the steel man habit: restate your opponent's view until they would endorse it themselves.
Only then attack — and watch how often the urge to attack evaporates.
Share this: restate one opinion you reject until its holder would say 'yes, that's it'.

items.title: Herd Mathematics
items.question: 'Everyone in my class is buying this phone, so I should too' is a deductively valid argument.
items.correctExplanation: Right — popularity drives no logical conclusion. The class could all be making the same mistake together.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. What the class buys has no logical power over what one should buy — that is the bandwagon fallacy wearing a school uniform. A valid argument needs premises that force the conclusion, not peer pressure.
items.lessonContent:
Bandwagon pressure exploits belonging: agreeing with the group feels safe and social.
Asch's conformity experiments showed people denying their own eyes to match a group.
Knowing the mechanism is half the defence; the other half is asking 'but is it true?'
First dissenters pay a social price — which is why they deserve attention, not mockery.
Share this: in your next group decision, be the one who asks what the group hasn't considered.

items.title: Name-Dropping Rule
items.question: Mentioning a person at any point during an argument automatically commits an ad hominem.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — the fallacy is replacing argument with attack, not merely naming a human.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. An ad hominem occurs only when personal traits are used as the reason to dismiss a claim. Quoting someone, praising them, or discussing their actions is not automatically an attack.
items.lessonContent:
Not every mention of a person is an attack on one — the fallacy needs the personal point to replace engagement.
Quoting, crediting and criticising conduct are all legitimate; substitution is the crime.
Crying 'ad hominem!' at every name is itself a conversation-stopper.
The category boundary matters: about the argument, or instead of it?
Share this: collect one example today of a name used as evidence and one used innocently.

items.title: The Weakened Clone
items.question: Refuting a weaker version of an opponent's claim counts as refuting their actual claim.
items.correctExplanation: Right — defeating a distorted copy defeats only the copy. The original claim walks away untouched.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Knocking down a weakened version of a position leaves the real position standing — that is exactly why the straw man is a fallacy. Refutation must engage what the opponent actually asserted.
items.lessonContent:
Refutation is target-locked: it defeats exactly what it engages, nothing more.
Defeating a distortion is a no-op against the original claim.
That is why honest debaters quote opponents verbatim before attacking.
Quote-then-attack is not politeness — it is accuracy.
Share this: next time you see a quote attacked, check the quote against the original source.

items.title: The Petrol Car
items.question: 'How can you trust Dr. Mehta's climate research? She drives a petrol car.' This attacks the arguer instead of the research.
items.correctExplanation: Yes — her driving habits are irrelevant to the data. The tactic shifts focus from the science to the scientist.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The reply ignores the research entirely and aims at the researcher's lifestyle — a textbook ad hominem. Her car choices cannot alter the measurements or the analysis.
items.lessonContent:
The hypocrisy jab feels devastating because hypocrisy is genuinely annoying — but annoyance is not logic.
A claim's truth is independent of its speaker's consistency.
Tu quoque — 'you too' — is the formal name when the attack is the accuser's own behaviour.
The real question survives the gotcha untouched.
Share this: enjoy one gotcha moment today, then ask what claim it actually disproved.

items.title: Bandwagon Twins
items.question: The bandwagon fallacy and the appeal to popularity are essentially the same error.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — both treat 'many people believe it' as if it were 'therefore it is true'.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The bandwagon image (jump on because everyone did) is just the folksy name for argumentum ad populum. The error is identical: crowd size substituting for evidence.
items.lessonContent:
The fallacy family has many names for cousin-moves: ad populum, bandwagon, appeal to the masses.
They share one core: crowd size offered as proof.
Learning the aliases sharpens spotting — the same trick wears different name-tags in ads, politics and group chats.
Once you see the skeleton, the costumes stop mattering.
Share this: name the fallacy family next time an ad counts its believers.

items.title: The Harsh Test
items.question: A straw man fallacy strengthens the original argument by stress-testing a harsher version of it.
items.correctExplanation: Right — the fallacy replaces the argument rather than testing it. Nothing about the original gets stronger.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A straw man does not test anything — it swaps the real claim for a caricature and attacks that. The original argument is simply never engaged, which is the whole deception.
items.lessonContent:
A stress-test strengthens an argument by surviving the strongest attack; a straw man dodges by attacking the weakest version.
The difference is direction of distortion — one goes harder than reality, the other softer and sillier.
Real critical thinking seeks the strongest form of an opponent's case.
Steel-manning is the discipline; straw-manning is the reflex.
Share this: take one view you reject and ask what its strongest version would say.

items.title: Nine Out of Ten
items.question: 'Nine out of ten dentists recommend this brand' is, all by itself, conclusive proof that the brand is best.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — an endorsement count is not proof. Which dentists, chosen how, compared to what?
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. A recommendation tally is weak testimony at best, never conclusive proof — the survey could be cherry-picked, sponsored, or vague. Notice the claim never says best among what alternatives.
items.lessonContent:
Endorsement statistics are testimony, and testimony's value depends on who, how many, and chosen how.
Sponsored surveys, cherry-picked panels and vague baselines all hollow the number out.
The question 'compared with what?' restores the missing baseline.
Dentist endorsements began as advertising's most successful formula — and remain its most parodied.
Share this: ask 'nine out of ten of whom?' about the next statistic you see.

items.title: Evidence versus Insults
items.question: Criticising the quality of someone's evidence is itself an ad hominem attack.
items.correctExplanation: Right — attacking the evidence is exactly what good argument is supposed to do.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. An ad hominem attacks the person; scrutinising their evidence targets the argument itself. 'Your sample was too small' is legitimate criticism, not a personal attack.
items.lessonContent:
Legitimate criticism targets premises, inferences and evidence — the three parts of any argument.
Personal attacks target a fourth thing that is not part of the argument at all.
Keeping the map straight is what separates scrutiny from smearing.
Reviewers and referees practise this separation professionally.
Share this: grade one argument today premise by premise and notice how little the author matters.

items.title: Centuries of Belief
items.question: The ad populum fallacy says that a claim's widespread acceptance, on its own, never proves the claim true.
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — popularity is not truth-tracking. Nearly everyone once believed the sun circled the earth.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The fallacy exists precisely because mass belief and truth are different things — continents of people have been confidently wrong for centuries. Acceptance needs evidence behind it to count as proof.
items.lessonContent:
Acceptance and truth vary independently: some true claims were long rejected, some falsehoods were long believed.
Continental drift was ridiculed for decades; geocentrism ruled for millennia.
The lesson is not cynicism — it is that belief needs evidence, not duration.
Long-standing consensus among informed experts earns trust; mere longevity does not.
Share this: find one thing 'everyone has always known' and check when it was last tested.

items.title: The Factory Phantom
items.question: Responding to 'we should recycle more' with 'so you want to shut down every factory' builds a straw man.
items.correctExplanation: Yes — the reply inflates a modest proposal into an absurd extreme, then attacks the extreme.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. 'Recycle more' never implied shutting down industry — the response invents a ridiculous version of the position and fights that instead. Inflating to an absurd extreme is the most common straw-manning move.
items.lessonContent:
The commonest straw-manning move is inflation: stretch 'some' into 'all', 'prefer' into 'obsess', 'regulate' into 'ban'.
The inflated version is always easier to mock, which is exactly the point.
Inflation-spotting is a learnable reflex: listen for 'so what you're saying is' and check the stretch.
The counter-move is restating the original scale before responding.
Share this: count the 'so you want to' inflations in one conversation this week.

items.title: The Truth Condition
items.question: An ad hominem fallacy only occurs when the personal attack is factually false.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — even a true personal fact is irrelevant if it is used to dismiss the argument.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The fallacy is in the irrelevance, not the falsity: 'he really did fail maths' still says nothing about his budget argument. A true fact deployed as a substitute for engagement is still an ad hominem.
items.lessonContent:
The ad hominem's flaw is relevance, not accuracy — even a true personal fact proves nothing about the argument.
A genuine failure decades ago still leaves today's reasoning untouched.
Fallacies are about connections: a true statement in the wrong place is still a wrong move.
Relevance is the master concept — most informal fallacies are relevance failures in costume.
Share this: when a true fact is dropped into a debate, ask what it is supposed to prove.

items.title: Unpleasant but Right
items.question: An argument can be rejected on solid logical grounds even when its proponent is thoroughly unpleasant.
items.correctExplanation: Right — validity depends on the argument's structure, not the arguer's personality.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. A rude person can present a flawless argument, and a saint can present a broken one. Judging the reasoning is separate from judging the person — that separation is what the ad hominem fallacy violates.
items.lessonContent:
Two independent judgements: the person (kind, consistent, pleasant?) and the argument (valid, sound?).
Conflating them is how bad arguments from good people slide by, and good arguments from bad people get dismissed.
Courts understood this long ago: even a criminal's testimony is weighed, not automatically discarded.
The separation feels cold and is actually fairness.
Share this: separate the messenger from the message in one judgement you make today.

items.title: The Friendship Motive
items.question: 'You only support this policy because your friends do' addresses the actual reasoning behind the policy.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — it speculates about motives while saying nothing about the policy's merits.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The reply is about why the person might hold the view, not whether the view is sound — a motive-focused sidestep. Even if the motive were true, the policy's arguments would stand or fall on their own.
items.lessonContent:
Explaining why someone holds a view is psychology; evaluating the view is logic.
Both can be done — but only one of them settles the argument.
Motive-talk is a spotlight shift: engaging, vivid, and silent about the actual claim.
Even a correct motive report leaves the claim's evidence exactly where it was.
Share this: catch one motive explanation today and re-ask the original question.

items.title: When Crowds Know
items.question: Appealing to what a crowd believes is always fallacious, even when the crowd consists of relevant experts.
items.correctExplanation: Right — expert consensus earned through evidence is testimony with weight, not head-counting.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. When specialists converge after examining evidence, citing that consensus is citing informed testimony — categorically different from 'everyone believes it, so true'. The ad populum fallacy targets popularity as proof, not expertise as evidence.
items.lessonContent:
Citing expert consensus differs from crowd-counting: the experts' numbers carry the weight of evidence behind them.
Astronomers agreeing the universe expands is testimony to data, not to popularity.
The carve-out has limits: it assumes genuine, independent convergence.
Asking why the experts agree upgrades the shortcut into understanding.
Share this: next time you cite a consensus, be ready to name one piece of evidence behind it.

items.title: Who Builds It
items.question: The straw man fallacy is committed by the person whose position gets misrepresented.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — the fallacy belongs to the misrepresenter, the one who builds and attacks the scarecrow.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. The victim's position is the raw material — the fallacy is committed by whoever distorts it. Being misrepresented makes you the target, not the culprit.
items.lessonContent:
Fallacies are committed, not suffered: the misrepresenter owns the straw man, not the misrepresented.
Keeping the arrow of blame straight matters when both sides accuse each other of the same move.
Ask 'who changed the claim?' and the culprit reveals itself.
Quotation is the currency of accountability in argument.
Share this: in the next dispute you witness, track who quoted and who paraphrased.

items.title: Empty but Loud
items.question: An ad populum argument can be emotionally persuasive while remaining logically empty.
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — that gap between persuasive power and logical content is what makes the fallacy dangerous.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. 'Everyone knows this' feels reassuring and requires no thinking, which is exactly why it persuades. Emotional pull and logical emptiness happily coexist — the fallacy works because it feels like belonging.
items.lessonContent:
Persuasion has many engines — emotion, belonging, repetition, confidence — and logic is only one of them.
A fallacy can be perfectly engineered persuasion while proving nothing.
Feeling convinced is data about you, not about the claim.
Advertisers and demagogues alike optimize for the feeling, not the proof.
Share this: notice one moment today when confidence, not evidence, moved you.

items.title: The Decay Gambit
items.question: 'My opponent wants less spending; clearly he wants this city to decay' is closest to a straw man.
items.correctExplanation: Yes — 'less spending' is quietly rewritten as 'wants decay', a much easier target to attack.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Wanting less spending does not mean wanting decay — the speaker substitutes a sinister motive for the actual position. That substitution-and-attack pattern is the straw man signature.
items.lessonContent:
Slipping a sinister motive into an opponent's position is straw-manning with a mask.
The fake motive is always more attackable than the real policy.
Watch for motive verbs — wants, hopes, plans — that the opponent never used.
The counter is asking them to state their own goal in their own words.
Share this: replace one assigned motive today with a direct question about intent.

items.title: Insult plus Proof
items.question: Calling an argument stupid is technically an ad hominem even when you also completely refute it.
items.correctExplanation: Right — the fallacy is abuse standing in for argument. Here the refutation does the actual work.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Rude packaging around a genuine refutation is bad manners, not a fallacy — the reasoning is still fully engaged. Ad hominem means the personal jab replaces engagement with the argument, not accompanies it.
items.lessonContent:
Rudeness alongside a full refutation is a manners problem, not a logic problem.
The fallacy label applies only when the jab substitutes for engagement.
This is why 'that's ad hominem!' sometimes loses arguments it should win — the refutation stands regardless.
Judging packaging and content separately is the mature skill.
Share this: separate one speaker's tone from their reasoning today and grade each on its own.

items.title: The Latin Label
items.question: The formal Latin name for the appeal-to-popularity fallacy is argumentum ad populum.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — 'argument to the people', the scholarly name for crowd-as-proof.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. Argumentum ad populum literally means 'argument to the people' — appealing to the crowd's beliefs as if numbers were evidence. Spotting the Latin label helps you notice the move in polished writing.
items.lessonContent:
Latin tags like argumentum ad populum are compression: a whole failure-pattern packed into a name.
Named patterns get spotted faster — the label primes the recognition.
The same holds for ad hominem ('to the person') and its many cousins.
Taxonomy is not pedantry; it is a spotting toolkit.
Share this: teach one fallacy name to someone today and watch them start seeing it everywhere.

items.title: Why It Works
items.question: Straw-manning often succeeds because the audience never heard the original position.
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — with no original for comparison, the caricature becomes the position in the audience's mind.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The distortion only fools listeners who lack the original for comparison — once you have heard both, the fake collapses. That is why checking primary sources defuses straw men so reliably.
items.lessonContent:
Straw men thrive on audiences that never heard the original — with nothing to compare, the caricature becomes the claim.
That is why secondhand summaries are the fallacy's natural habitat.
The antidote is primary sources: read the speech, not the tweet about the speech.
Verification beats eloquence in any serious disagreement.
Share this: read one primary source behind a summary you consumed today.

items.title: The Spotlight Shift
items.question: An ad hominem turns the spotlight from the claim onto the claimant.
items.correctExplanation: Right — that redirect is the entire mechanics of the fallacy: judge the person, forget the point.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is True. The move works by changing the subject of the sentence — from 'is this claim true?' to 'what is wrong with this person?' Once the spotlight moves, the original question quietly disappears.
items.lessonContent:
An ad hominem changes the sentence's subject: from 'is the claim true?' to 'what is wrong with the claimer?'
Once the spotlight moves, the original question quietly exits the stage.
Noticing the redirect half-defuses it — drag the light back to the claim.
Interviewers and moderators earn their keep by exactly this move.
Share this: in one debate today, name the moment the subject changed from claim to person.

items.title: Experts versus Crowds
items.question: Believing a claim because most qualified experts accept it after reviewing evidence is the ad populum fallacy.
items.correctExplanation: Correct — that is deferring to informed consensus, which is evidence-based testimony, not head-counting.
items.incorrectExplanation: It is False. Ad populum counts noses regardless of knowledge; expert consensus carries the weight of training and evidence behind it. Trusting qualified consensus is reasonable shorthand, not a fallacy — though checking why experts agree is even better.
items.lessonContent:
One question separates healthy deference from the bandwagon: what generated the agreement?
Evidence-examined convergence earns trust; fashion, fear and follower counts do not.
It is also fine to ask both: what do the experts say, and why do they say it?
The 'why' is where your own judgment gets trained.
Share this: next time you defer to consensus, spend thirty seconds on the why.
